Cardiology and hematology · published research

Vasoconstriction

One microswine experiment found acute widening of arteries after local laser delivery to histamine-induced spasm. No clinical study has tested this effect in people.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One microswine experiment found acute widening of arteries after local laser delivery to histamine-induced spasm. No clinical study has tested this effect in people.

Summary of the Evidence

One direct publication examined light treatment for vasoconstriction. It was an in-vivo experiment in ten atherosclerotic Yucatan microswine, with histamine-induced spasm assessed in 13 arteries. No independent replication, patient study, or separate cell experiment is filed under this indication. The study tests reversal of an experimentally induced arterial spasm, not chronic vasoconstrictive disease.

Human and clinical evidence

No human intervention study was identified. The experiment did not involve people with Raynaud syndrome, coronary spasm, or another clinical vasoconstrictive disorder.

Animal evidence

Gal et al. reproduced histamine-induced narrowing in the microswine arteries and then delivered light percutaneously through fiber optics to the spasm site. Visible red 632 nm light completely reversed narrowing in two of four treated arteries and reduced it in the other two. Near-infrared 1,064 nm light also reduced narrowing in all three tested arteries. Sham fiber-optic trials did not produce comparable relaxation. The experiment involved only a few arteries per wavelength, so it cannot establish which wavelength works best or how long the response lasts (Gal et al. 1992).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate in-vitro or ex-vivo publication is included for this indication. The article refers to earlier laboratory work on vascular smooth-muscle tension, but those experiments are not independent records in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study compared ultraviolet 351 nm, visible red 632 nm, and near-infrared 1,064 nm light. Ultraviolet exposure is outside the usual red and near-infrared PBM ranges and should not be grouped with them as equivalent treatment. Light was delivered directly to the induced spasm through percutaneous fiber optics, with angiography used to observe the acute response. The database does not provide a comparable fluence or enough dosimetry to define a clinical protocol. No dose-finding or patient delivery study was identified.

Interpretation

The experiment shows that catheter-delivered red and near-infrared light can relax histamine-induced spasm in some microswine arteries under the tested conditions. It does not establish a durable effect or treatment for vasoconstrictive disease in people. The result remains a single animal experiment requiring replication.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reversing arterial spasm in people
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One microswine experiment found acute vessel relaxation after local light delivery, but no human study or independent replication is listed. The finding applies to chemically induced spasm under catheter-based delivery. Repeating the experiment with a prespecified dose and longer observation would clarify the response before considering whether a safe human delivery route exists.
